name: Greenish Glaucous
lede: Greenish Glaucous is a pale, powdery sage, named by modifier grammar as greenish plus [[dusty-blue]], and placed on Ridgway's 1912 color plates before the ISCC-NBS dictionary filed it in 1955.

sections.title: Greenish, plus a plant's bloom
sections.body:
The parent word, [[dusty-blue]], describes the dusty blue-grey-green bloom on a leaf, grape or plum skin, and Greenish Glaucous simply pushes that word further toward [[green]] [1]. Robert Ridgway, an American ornithologist, gave it plate XLI, hue 33‴, tone f, in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, a scan of an aged printed page and so only approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 later filed the same name at block 148 [1][2].

It is close enough to [[pale-green-grey|Pale green grey]] that our data treats the two as a near-duplicate, zero color-distance units apart [3]. Beyond that exact match, the nearest look-alikes are [[corydalis-green|Corydalis Green]], a shade yellower, and [[pale-niagara-green|Pale Niagara Green]], greener [3]. A separate 1930 source, Maerz and Paul's dictionary, records almost the same color under the name Starling's Egg Green, first listed in 1902, on their plate 27 B 2 [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our 23,781-painting archive, 280 paintings carry a color close enough to this one over enough of their canvas to count, 1.18 per cent, as photographed, more common than 72 per cent of our named colors [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, by lightness rank within each painting, in 56 per cent of the 280 paintings where that lens applies, so varnish cannot fake the reading [5].

It peaks in the 1800s, found in 1.4 per cent of the 8,345 paintings we have from that century (115 paintings), 1.4 times the expected rate [5]. Alfred Sisley is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 8 of the 50 of his works in our archive, 7.5 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [5]. It is also strongly tied to Rajput painting and to Impressionism as styles [5]. The earliest match is dated 1462, in a work attributed to Andrea Mantegna, though the archive's thin early centuries make that a floor, not a first sighting, and 450 years older than Ridgway's 1912 record of the name [5].
